lead: Link‑state routing floods a complete view of the network and then each router runs Dijkstra’s Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm. The idea is to avoid the slow convergence of distance‑vector protocols and to compute optimal routes from a single source. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is the most widely used link‑state protocol in enterprise and ISP networks.
prereq: You need: Routing basics and Distance vector routing.

blocks.text: Each OSPF router creates a Link‑State Advertisement (LSA). An LSA lists the router's interfaces, the cost of each attached link, and the neighbor router IDs.
The cost is a numeric value that is inversely proportional to the bandwidth of the link. By default cost = 10⁸ ÷ bandwidth (bits per second).
When a router generates a new LSA, it sends the LSA to all OSPF‑enabled interfaces.
All neighbors forward the LSA to their neighbors. This process is called flooding.
Flooding continues until every router in the same OSPF area has a copy of the LSA.

items: Sequence number in the LSA prevents old copies from overwriting newer ones.
Acknowledgement packet confirms receipt of each LSA.

blocks.text: The collection of LSAs forms a complete topology map of the area.
Only routers inside the same area exchange LSAs. This limits the size of the database.

sections.h3: Cost calculation and Shortest Path First (SPF)

blocks.text: After flooding, each router runs Dijkstra’s SPF algorithm on its local link‑state database.

items: Set the source router’s distance to 0 and all other distances to ∞.
Initially the visited set is empty; the source will be selected first because its distance is 0, then marked visited.
Select the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance.
Update the distance of each neighbor: new = distance(u) + cost(u,v) where u is the node just selected as visited.
If new < current neighbor distance, replace it and record the predecessor.
Mark the selected node as visited.
Repeat until all nodes are visited.

blocks.text: The predecessor table yields a shortest‑path tree rooted at the source router.
From the tree, the router extracts the next‑hop for every destination network.

blocks.where: d(v) is the tentative distance to node v; cost(u,v) is the link cost between u and v.

blocks.text: OSPF uses the tree to install routes in the routing table. The route entry contains destination prefix, next‑hop IP address, and total cost.
An OSPF network is divided into areas. Area 0 is the backbone. All other areas must connect to the backbone.
Area boundaries limit LSA flooding. Routers that have interfaces in more than one area are called Area Border Routers (ABR).
ABRs generate summary LSAs. A summary LSA advertises the total cost to reach networks in other OSPF areas without revealing the internal topology.
The design reduces memory and CPU load on routers deep inside an area.

items: Virtual links can connect a non‑backbone area to the backbone when a physical link is missing.

blocks.text: In Indian campuses, OSPF areas often separate academic blocks, hostels, and data‑center zones to keep the LSA database small.

examples.question: Using the graph above, compute the shortest‑path tree from router 1 with OSPF SPF. List the next‑hop and total cost for destinations 2, 3, and 4.
steps: Initialize distances: d(1)=0, d(2)=∞, d(3)=∞, d(4)=∞.
Visit node 1. Update neighbors: d(2)=0+10=10, d(3)=0+5=5.
Select unvisited node with smallest distance: node 3 (5).
Visit node 3. Update neighbor 4: new cost =5+9=14 → d(4)=14.
Select next smallest unvisited node: node 2 (10).
Visit node 2. Update neighbor 4: new cost =10+2=12 → d(4)=12 (replace 14).
Next‑hop for 2 is 2, for 3 is 3, for 4 is 2.
examples.answer: To 2 → via 2 (cost 10); to 3 → via 3 (cost 5); to 4 → via 2 (cost 12).

traps: Assuming the LSA flood itself computes the shortest path. Flooding only distributes topology; SPF runs later.
Using the cost of the opposite direction for a undirected link. OSPF treats the cost as symmetric, but the example uses the same value both ways.
Updating a neighbor’s distance with the old distance of the source node. Dijkstra always uses the already finalised distance of the visited node.
Confusing area‑border summarization with intra‑area SPF. Summaries are used only between areas, not inside the SPF calculation shown.

quiz.q: What does LSA stand for in OSPF?
Why does OSPF limit LSA flooding to a single area?
quiz.a: To keep the link‑state database small, reduce CPU load, and limit the amount of control traffic.

quiz.q: A link between routers A and B has bandwidth 100 Mbps. Compute the OSPF default cost for this link.
quiz.a: Cost = 10⁸ ÷ 100 000 000 = 1. So the default cost is 1.

quiz.q: Using the topology in the figure, list the next‑hop for router 4 to reach router 1.
quiz.a: Router 4’s shortest‑path tree to 1 goes via router 2 (cost 12). The next‑hop is router 2.

quiz.q: If a link cost changes from 10 to 3 after an LSA update, explain how OSPF converges to the new shortest‑path tree.
quiz.a: The router attached to the changed link generates a new LSA with the updated cost. Flooding distributes the LSA to all routers in the area. Each router discards the old LSA (lower sequence number) and runs SPF again on the updated database. The new tree reflects the lower cost, and routing tables are updated accordingly.

quiz.q: Name the OSPF area that must connect all other areas.
What is the role of an ABR in OSPF?
quiz.a: An Area Border Router connects two or more OSPF areas, forwards LSAs between them, and generates summary LSAs for inter‑area routing.

quiz.q: A network engineer wants to reduce SPF computation time on a large campus. Which OSPF feature should they use?
quiz.a: Divide the campus into multiple OSPF areas so each router stores a smaller link‑state database and runs SPF on a limited topology.

beyond: Not for the exam. OSPF is being extended with Segment Routing to simplify path encoding. Researchers explore using SDN controllers to inject LSAs for traffic engineering. Cloud providers often run OSPF inside virtual networks to keep compatibility with on‑premise sites. For the next step, look at IS‑IS, another link‑state protocol used in large service provider backbones.
